--- title: "The Daily Dose" subtitle: "Turning an old workout log into a Shiny for Python app" author: "Martin Frigaard" date: "2026-08-05" categories: [Python, Shiny] image: "image.png" draft: false toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-title: 'Contents' toc-location: right ---
I started storing my daily workouts on GitHub in 2020, and continued until about 2024. I logged almost every workout I did (1,001 total). In this post I'll cover how that log became [`daily-dose`](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/daily-dose), a small Shiny for Python app. We'll walk through the app's history, its architecture, and some design choices I made to keep it small. ![The Daily Dose app](image.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"} ## Where the log came from The log started as an R Markdown site in early 2022. Each year had its own page, and each workout sat under a dated `###` heading. Most entries were typed in markdown, but for a stretch of 2020, the workouts lived on a whiteboard, so I took a picture the board instead. By 2024 I had 881 typed entries and 120 photos. I eventually noticed that I'd organized date (specifically), but I rarely browsed it year by year. I decided I wanted an app that could do two things: select a random workout, and look at what I did on **this** date in past years. I rebuilt the website as [Shiny for Python](https://shiny.posit.co/py/) app-package on top. ## How the pieces fit I wanted the app to do the two things covered above (and nothing else). I thought of this in three layers: a build script, a pure Python core, and a thin Shiny app. The diagram below shows how a workout moves from its original source to the screen. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%% flowchart TD subgraph Src["Original log"] Rmd[/"Typed .Rmd entries"/] Photos[/"Whiteboard photos"/] end subgraph Build["build_workouts_data.py"] Parse("Parse dates
and checkboxes") Shrink("Rotate, resize,
save as JPEG") Dedup{"Text and photo
on one date?"} end subgraph Pkg["daily_dose package"] Json[("workouts.json")] Imgs[("www/images/")] Core[["core.py"]] end subgraph App["Shiny app"] Server("app.py") Card[["workout_card()"]] end Rmd -->|"i. read markdown"| Parse Photos -->|"ii. read png"| Shrink Parse --> Dedup Shrink --> Dedup Dedup -->|"iii. text wins"| Json Dedup -->|"iii. photo kept"| Imgs Json --> Core Core -->|"iv. launch app"| Server Server --> Card Imgs -.-> Card style Src fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style Build font-size:15px,fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style Pkg fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style App fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style Parse fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Shrink fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Dedup fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Core fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Server fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Card fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF ``` The build script runs by hand, only when the source files change. It writes every workout to a single JSON file that ships inside the package. The app reads that file once at startup. The core is just two functions over a list of records. `random_workout()` picks one record, and `on_this_day()` returns every record that matches today's month and day: ```python def on_this_day(workouts, today=None): target = today or date.today() matches = [ w for w in workouts if int(w["date"][5:7]) == target.month and int(w["date"][8:10]) == target.day ] return sorted(matches, key=lambda w: w["date"], reverse=True) ``` ## Design choices As I mentioned above, the workouts were stored as markdown text and images. Below I'll cover how I dealt with these two types of files, and what I did to handle duplicates. ### One record shape I could've have kept the markdown entries and photos in two collections, but I decided every workout would just be one record with a `date` and a `kind` (`"text"` or `"image"`). Both core functions work on a flat list without caring what the record holds. Only `workout_card()` checks `kind`, because only the card has to draw it. ### Text wins on shared dates Some of the 2020 workouts had *both* a photo *and* a typed entry for the same session (don't ask me how). Keeping both would show one workout twice under **On This Day**. It would also give those dates double the odds in a random pick. I decided to preferentially write the build script to keep the typed entry, since these usually recorded the sets and reps (and the photo didn't). ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%% flowchart TD Entry(["Next entry
(text or image)"]) Seen{"Date already
stored?"} Swap{"Stored entry is an image
and this one is text?"} Store("Store this entry") Skip("Keep stored entry,
drop this one") Out[("One entry per date")] Entry --> Seen Seen -->|"no"| Store Seen -->|"yes"| Swap Swap -->|"yes"| Store Swap -->|"no"| Skip Store --> Out Skip --> Out style Entry fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style Seen fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Swap fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Store fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Skip fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Out fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 ``` ### Keep the markdown as written I thought I'd be able to categorize the workout by type, but over the four years, I never settled on one markdown format for exercises or reps. Forcing them into structured fields would risk mangling any entry the parser misread. So the parser pulls out only the date and the done checkbox and keeps the rest verbatim. The parser also fails loudly. Any line that looks like a date heading but doesn't match the strict pattern stops the build. I've found this to be better than silently merging that line into the entry above it. ### A core without Shiny `core.py` never imports `shiny`, so it keeps both functions testable with plain `pytest`, with no running app. It also leaves `app.py` as thin glue: two buttons, two effects, and one render function. ```{mermaid} %%| fig-width: 6 %%| fig-align: 'center' %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': { 'fontFamily': 'monospace', "darkMode":false}}}%% flowchart TD User(["User clicks
button"]) subgraph ShinyGrp["Imports shiny"] AppPy("app.py
buttons, effects, render") Card[["workout_card()"]] end subgraph CoreGrp["Plain Python (core.py)"] Load[["load_workouts()"]] Rand[["random_workout()"]] Today[["on_this_day()"]] end Tests(["pytest
tests/"]) User --> AppPy AppPy --> Rand AppPy --> Today Load --> AppPy AppPy --> Card Tests -.-> Load Tests -.-> Rand Tests -.-> Today style ShinyGrp fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style CoreGrp font-size:15px,fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px,rx:10,ry:10 style User fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style Tests fill:#FFFFFF,color:#000000,stroke:#333 style AppPy fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF,rx:5,ry:5 style Card fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Load fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Rand fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF style Today fill:#4CBB9D,color:#FFFFFF ``` I'm still new to Shiny for Python, so I used Shiny Core rather than Express, which keeps the UI and server in separate, explicit objects. ### Smaller photos The original photos were phone PNGs, about 325MB for 120 images. Since the app ships as an installable package, the build script rotates, resizes, and saves each one as JPEG. The total dropped to about 21MB with no visible loss on handwriting. ### A shim for deployment The app runs on [Posit Connect Cloud](https://docs.posit.co/connect-cloud/), which expects `app.py` and `requirements.txt` at the repo root. The package uses a `src` layout, so the root `app.py` is a small shim that imports the real app. :::: {.callout-warning collapse='false' appearance='default' icon=false} ## [`requirements.txt`]{style='font-weight: bold; font-size: 1.15em;'} ::: {style='font-size: 1.10em; color: #282b2d;'} My first `requirements.txt` held only `-e .`, which failed because Connect Cloud can't resolve an editable install. It now lists the dependencies directly. ::: :::: ## Recap The `daily-dose` app-package successfully kept the two features I used and dropped the rest. I found processing the data (turning typed entries and photos into one record shape) in a Shiny-free core made the logic easy to test. I just used Shiny as a thin layer to put the outputs on the screen. Also--writing the documentation in [`great-docs`](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-docs/) was intuitive and fun because I use Quarto quite a bit. * [App on Posit Connect Cloud](https://mjfrigaard-daily-dose.share.connect.posit.cloud/) * [Repo](https://github.com/mjfrigaard/daily-dose) * [Docs](https://mjfrigaard.github.io/daily-dose/)
